3.4 — Projectile Damage, Tuning & Playtest

Your turret sees you, aims, and fires on a timer — and every bullet passes cleanly through your body, because the projectile is still just a picture. Today you close the loop: give the bullet a body, detect the hit, apply damage through the method you already wrote, clean up. Then you take control of the numbers that decide whether the encounter is tense or unfair.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make my bullet hurt the player?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

My bullets should actually hurt the player, and the fight should be hard without being unfair.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the bullet a bodywhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat (the collider-and-trigger recipe), and the Rigidbody2D row of this lesson's reference table
  2. Detect the hit, and confirm what was hitwhat does this part do?Read: the OnTriggerEnter2D, OnCollisionEnter2D and CompareTag rows of this lesson's reference table
  3. Apply the damage through the health method you already wrotewhat does this part do?Read: 2.2 — Spikes: Physics, Damage & Death (the method you wrote there), and the GetComponent and public-method rows of this lesson's reference table
  4. Destroy the bulletwhat does this part do?Read: 3.2 — Projectiles: Instantiate, Fire, Destroy, and the Destroy row of this lesson's reference table

Three of these four parts are lessons you have already finished, and the fourth is the one genuinely new idea: until now, every script you wrote changed its own values. A bullet has to reach into a different object and ask that object to change its own number — which is a question about access, not about arithmetic.

The split is finished when every part names something you could point at in the editor: a component on a prefab, a callback, a method on a script, a call. If a part needs the word "and" twice to describe it, it is two parts.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Trigger or solid — which did you choose for the bullet, and what does that choice cost you? Name the checkbox and the callback name that have to agree, and what the Console does when they do not.

The projectile prefab is tagged Enemy, the same tag the turret that fired it carries. What will your callback actually test for, and on which object does it ask?

2.1 is this lesson in different clothes: confirm the thing that triggered was a coin, change the count, destroy the object. Which line of your 2.1 pickup is the same move as today's tag check, and which line is the same move as today's destroy?

In 2.2 you wrote a method on PlayerController that takes a signed amount and changes health. Until today, nothing outside that file ever called it. How does one object call a method on another — and what does that method have to be made into before the call can even be written?

3.2 already ended with a Destroy on the bullet. What is different about destroying it on a hit instead of on a timer, and what has to be true before the destroy line is allowed to run?

The Problem: A Bullet With No Body ~15 min

Your goal: being shot should cost you health. Three things have to be true before it can. Something must give the bullet a shape. Something must notice that the shape met the player. And something must turn "met the player" into a change in a number. Go and find out which of the three is missing.

Select Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile in the Project window and read its Inspector. Then select the Player and read its Inspector. Write down what each one has, and what the bullet is missing.

The rule from 2.1 still runs this project. Overlap messages only fire when the two objects both have a Collider2D and at least one of them also has a Rigidbody2D. That is why the projectile being "only a Transform and a Sprite Renderer" is fatal rather than cosmetic. It is also why a bullet may not need a body of its own: the Player has carried one since 2.2. Check that reasoning against the rule rather than assuming it.

Before you add anything, decide what kind of collider a bullet should have. Here are the honest options:

Setup for the bulletWhat the player feelsWhat firesWhat it costs
Collider with Is Trigger ticked The bullet passes into you and reports the hit without touching your movement. OnTriggerEnter2D You must give the bullet a collider and size it by hand — a default collider is sized from the sprite's import bounds, and this prefab is scaled. A pass-through bullet also cannot be blocked by a wall later without more work.
Solid collider (Is Trigger off) The bullet thuds into you. If your player's body is Dynamic, it can shove them. OnCollisionEnter2D Now the bullet is an obstacle. A fast, thin, solid collider moved by transform is exactly the tunnelling case from 2.2: at high speed it can skip past a thin target in one frame.
Trigger collider + a Rigidbody2D on the bullet Same as the trigger row, but the bullet is now under simulation. OnTriggerEnter2D (and a body you can steer) One more component per bullet, and a body that will obey gravity unless you change its Gravity Scale. Buy this only if your bullet needs physics — bouncing, drag, or collision with walls.

The second decision is whose script runs the check. Both answers are defendable:

Where the hit check livesWhat it looks likeWhen it winsWhat it costs
On Projectile.cs The bullet implements the callback, identifies what it hit, and asks that thing to take damage. Each hazard carries its own behaviour. A bullet that later becomes a fireball changes only its own file, and a hazard you delete takes its damage code with it. Every projectile needs a way to reach the health of whatever it hit.
On PlayerController.cs The player implements the callback and works out what just hit them. One file shows everything in the game that can hurt the player — which is where a shield or invulnerability power-up will eventually live. Every new hazard needs another branch in the player's file, and the player's script grows without limit.

Socratic: Choosing a Hit Model

  1. Which of the two scripts will you put the hit check in, and what does that choice cost you later when the game has arrows, boss lasers and a flamethrower?
  2. A bullet that stops the player dead like a brick wall would be miserable to play against. Which of the three bullet setups avoids that, and what is the exact checkbox responsible?
  3. The projectile prefab is tagged Enemy, just like the turret and the mobile enemy. Given that, how will a bullet ever know it hit the player — whose tag will you actually test, and on which object?
  4. Your player's health method from 2.2 takes a signed amount. Which sign hurts — check the arithmetic in your own method rather than guessing — and what would happen if you passed the other one by mistake?
  5. What happens if you never call Destroy on the bullet? Describe the scene after a two-minute firefight and name the two systems that suffer first.
  6. A bullet in flight is a hazard even after it has left the turret's range. Is that correct behaviour for this game, or should a bullet stop mattering when the turret loses track of you? Argue it.
Read the Docs: The API for Landing a Hit ~15 min

This is the level-3 substitute for a walkthrough. The API is laid out below and the code is not: you write the file. Between them, these rows are the whole job — a callback, a tag check, a lookup, a call, a destroy, and two declarations. Every one of them costs something, so name the cost before you pick; otherwise you are not choosing, you are guessing.

APISignatureWhat you getWhat it costs
OnTriggerEnter2D void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) — a callback. Unity calls it; you never do. Fires on the first frame two shapes overlap, with Is Trigger ticked on at least one of them. The parameter is the other object's collider. Triggers only, and it fires once per entry — the shapes have to separate and meet again for a second message. A misspelling in the name is not an error; it is silence.
OnCollisionEnter2D void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision) — a callback Fires the moment two solid colliders meet, provided one of the two objects carries a Dynamic body. The parameter is the other object's collision. A different parameter type, so the tag is asked of collision.gameObject rather than the collider itself. A solid bullet is an obstacle: it shoves a Dynamic player instead of passing through. And a Kinematic body produces no contact message against a static collider at all — it passes through walls in silence.
Collider2D.CompareTag bool CompareTag(string tag) Asks the engine whether that object carries the tag. One check, and you know what kind of thing you hit. Exact spelling, and the tag has to exist in the project first. It must be asked of the object that carries the collider — other.gameObject or collision.gameObject — never of the script the callback lives on.
GetComponent<T>() T GetComponent<T>(), called on a GameObject or a component The component of that type on the object you call it on — here, the PlayerController that owns the health. A tag names the kind of thing; this is what tells you what it can do. It is a search, and it returns null when the type is not there. The plain version does not look at children, so the component has to sit on the object you actually touched. InParent and InChildren variants exist and cost you a slower search.
Calling a public method on another component player.TakeDamage(damage); — a call on a reference to another script, not a member of this class. The name is whatever you called yours in 2.2. Hands the problem to the object that owns the data: the bullet never touches the health number, it only asks. The method you wrote in 2.2 is declared private, so nothing outside PlayerController can see it yet. Widening it to public is part of today's work — and everything public becomes part of your game's interface, which is a promise to every future caller. Read your own method before you pass a number: a sign that is backwards is not a compiler error, it is a heal.
Destroy(Object) void Destroy(Object obj) Removes the object at the end of the frame — the same cleanup 3.2 used on a timer, now on a hit. It is final, and it is deferred: the object is still alive for the rest of the frame, which is why a hit can be counted twice if you do not also stop the callback from running again.
[SerializeField] private int A field declaration, not a call — the form you have used since 1.3. Class body, never inside a method. The name and the starting value are yours to choose. A named value that survives every frame and appears in the Inspector as the designer's tuning knob for how punishing one hit is. The type has to match the parameter of the method you call. TakeDamage(int amount) takes an int, so a float knob cannot be passed without a conversion the compiler will refuse.
Rigidbody2D A component you add to an object, not a call The component that puts an object into the physics simulation. A trigger pair reports nothing unless one of the two objects carries one — which is why your choice in the first table decides whether the bullet needs a body at all. A Dynamic body obeys gravity and is stopped by walls. Adding one changes what the bullet does, not merely whether it is detected — so buy it only if the setup you chose asks for it, and set its Gravity Scale deliberately.
Debug.Log(object) void Debug.Log(object message) Prints to the Console — the only feedback this game has until Unit 5. Text only, and it prints when you call it. A hit that lands and changes nothing prints nothing unless you print it yourself.
Four facts a signature cannot carry. First, the callback is silent about your mistakes: leave the collider off, mistype the method name, or tick the wrong checkbox, and the Console stays empty — "no error at all" is the hardest bug in this unit to find, which is why you check the component before you check the code. Second, the tag check is the first filter and the component lookup is the second: the only objects that reach the lookup are the ones your tag already let through, and a lookup that finds nothing hands you null rather than stopping the script, so every line below it has to be written as though the lookup succeeded. Third, the player's health lives on PlayerController and nowhere else — that is where you put it in 2.2, and the method that changes it is still private until you widen it. Fourth, the health method takes a signed amount on purpose, and the sign is decided by your own arithmetic rather than by convention: read the line in your method that changes health, work out which sign hurts, and pass that one. The same method then serves the spike, the bullet, and any healing source you add later, because a signed amount can travel in both directions.

Predict Before Building

  1. A tag check tells you what kind of thing you hit; a component lookup tells you what that thing can do. Which one do you need before you can hurt the player — and could today's callback be written with only the other one?
  2. The lookup hands back null when the object you hit carries no such component. What does the next line do with that null if you skip the guard, what does the Console point at, and why is the error message a worse teacher than the guard would have been?
  3. Your health method takes a signed amount. Who will call that same method in Unit 5, when a pickup starts healing you — and what would separate Heal and Hurt methods have cost you then?
  4. Inside the callback, the object your script sits on and the object you collided with are two different things. Which one do you destroy, and what would you be deleting by mistake if you got it backwards?
  5. A bullet has to report a hit without shoving the player anywhere. Which setup in the first table behaves like that, and which checkbox is responsible?
Build Lab: Close the Loop ~25 min

This one is on you, and there is no code in this section on purpose. A collider and a trigger are 2.1, a method that changes health is 2.2, a clone that destroys itself is 3.2, and a tag check is all three. What is new is the decision — and the specification below names the component, the callback, the method and the question to answer. The reference table names the API. The rest is yours.

Architectural specification: the body.
  • Which of the three setups in the first table did you choose — trigger, solid, or trigger plus a body — and what exactly does each one add to Turret_Projectile? Write your choice down before you open the prefab.
  • The prefab carries a Transform and a Sprite Renderer and nothing else. Which of the two missing components does your choice actually require — and which object in the pair is going to carry the Rigidbody2D, the bullet you are editing or the player who has had one since 2.2? Check both Inspectors before you answer, and say what your answer costs you per shot.
  • Open the Turret_Projectile prefab. The sprite is scaled and may sit on a child object — how do you size the collider so it matches what the player sees, and how do you confirm that in the Scene view rather than by guessing?
  • Is Is Trigger ticked or not? State it deliberately, out loud. The checkbox and the callback name have to agree, and the Console will not tell you when they do not.
Architectural specification: the hit.
  • Which callback method receives the message — and does its name depend on the checkbox you just set? What is the parameter's type in each case?
  • Which object's tag do you ask about, and which property carries it in each of the two callbacks?
  • What tag does the player actually carry, and where do you verify that rather than assume it?
  • Which lookup gets you from the object you hit to the script that owns the health — plain, InParent, or InChildren? Why is the plain one the right call here?
  • Why is the tag check the first filter, rather than looking for the script straight away? Say what each of the two checks actually tells you.
Architectural specification: the damage.
  • Which method do you call on the player, and which sign is the number you pass? Read the line in your own method that changes health before you answer — then say out loud what the other sign would do instead.
  • That method is private in the file you wrote in 2.2. What has to change in PlayerController.cs before another script can call it at all — and what does making it public commit you to for the rest of the year?
  • What guard protects the call when the lookup came back null, and what does the Console show without it?
  • Your damage knob is a serialized field on the bullet. What type must it match to work with the health method, and what default do you ship given the player's starting health? Justify the ratio, not just the number.
  • What message do you print so you can watch the health change with no UI at all?
Architectural specification: the cleanup.
  • Which object gets destroyed — the bullet, the player, or the object you hit? What happens to your health if you destroy the wrong one?
  • Where in the callback does the destroy line go: before the damage, or after it? What happens if the bullet survives a frame while still inside the player?
  • 3.2 ended with this same call on a timer. Why does the bullet need both a lifetime and this line — what is each one for, and which would you lose first?
  • What is sitting in the Hierarchy after a two-minute firefight if you never write the destroy line at all — and which two systems in your game slow down first?
Do not reach for a manager. There is a StatManager.cs in Assets/Scripts. It is empty, it has no health in it, and it has no method to change anything. Health lives on PlayerController, where you put it in 2.2, and it stays there. You will meet the manager again in 5.3, when a scene change finally gives you a reason to move your stats.

Save, wire nothing new, and press Play. Stand in front of a turret and let it shoot you. Your health number should fall by exactly your damage knob, the bullet should vanish, and when health reaches zero your death rule from 2.2 should fire. If the Console is silent, check the collider before you check the code — and check the tag spelling before you check the collider.

Read the Docs: The Difficulty Knobs ~15 min

Difficulty is not a feeling, it is a short list of numbers — and the numbers are not Unity's, they are yours. Every field in the table below is one you declared in this unit: the range you exposed in 3.1, the timing field you chose a method for in 3.3, the speed and the damage knob on the projectile. There are no correct values in this project, so the standard is not "right" — it is the player experience you can defend in one sentence.

The knobWhere your field livesWhat it controlsTense, and fairUnfairYour value
Detection range the field you exposed in TurretController.cs in 3.1 How much of the map is a danger zone. The player can see the turret before the turret sees the player. The first hit is always a surprise, and evasion looks impossible.
Fire cooldown the field your chosen timing method guards in TurretController.cs The gap the player gets between shots. There is a beat between shots to move in. A bullet hose with no room to dodge.
Projectile speed the field on Projectile.cs from 3.2 How much reaction time the player has. Dodgeable by a player who is watching. Faster than a human can react — the hit lands before the decision does.
Damage the [SerializeField] knob you declared today How punishing one mistake is, out of the player's total health. A mistake the player can recover from and learn from. One mistake ends the run, so there is no lesson in it.

There is a fifth knob, and nobody hands it to you: the one you invent. Look at your own Projectile.cs and TurretController.cs and find a number you could add that would change how the encounter feels — a muzzle offset, a lifetime, a spread. Name it, declare it as a serialized field, and put it in the table above with your own two adjectives next to it.

Architectural specification: build three turret personalities. The Overworld scene already contains two Turret instances — count them in the Hierarchy before you assume anything. If you want a third personality, duplicate one of the existing two (Ctrl+D); that gives you three. Do not duplicate both.
  • Which of the two existing turrets will keep its current numbers, and where in the scene does it sit?
  • For each personality you build, write down every value before you type it, and say what player experience you are aiming at in one sentence.
  • Inspector values on an instance override the prefab's values. Where do your personality numbers live — on the prefab, or on the instance in the Overworld? What happens to the other instance if you edit the prefab instead?
  • Does a personality need to be a different prefab, or just a different set of numbers on an instance? What does your answer cost you when you want to reuse a personality in another scene?
  • Which of your three personalities is the one you would hand a first-time player first, and which number would you change to prove it?
Bug Hunt: Silent Bullets ~15 min

Bug Hunt: Silent Bullets

  1. Leave the prefab without a collider and fire at yourself. What does the Console show? Why is "no error at all" harder to debug than a crash?
  2. Now tick Is Trigger on the bullet but keep the callback you wrote for collisions. Does anything fire? Which pair of checkbox and method name must match?
  3. Comment out the Destroy line and stand in front of a turret for thirty seconds. Count the objects in the Hierarchy in play mode. Which two systems in your game slow down first?
  4. Remove the null guard before you call the health method, then shoot a wall or another bullet. What error appears, and which line points at it?
  5. Set your damage knob to match the player's full starting health. What is the encounter now — and why is a one-hit kill a design statement rather than a bug?
  6. Delete the tag check and let the bullet damage anything it touches. What would go wrong the day the player can shoot back, and why is a whitelist safer than a blacklist here?
Playtest ~20 min

Swap seats with a partner and run a silent playtest — the 2.4 rules: you watch, they play, nobody speaks. Watch for:

  • Did they notice the turret before it fired, or was the first hit a surprise?
  • Did they try to dodge the bullets, or just sprint through the damage?
  • Which of your turret personalities was most satisfying to evade — and which one made them stop trying?
  • Did they ever work out what the detection range was, or did it feel random to them?

Tinker: One Knob at a Time

  1. From your partner's feedback, change exactly one number. Retest with the same partner. Did the experience improve, and can you point at the moment it changed?
  2. Change two numbers at once and retest. Why can you no longer say which change did the work? Write the rule down in one sentence.
  3. Make a bullet that is slow but huge and deadly, and one that is fast but weak. Which reads as more fair to a player, and what does that tell you about reaction time as a design resource?
  4. Commit and push: "3.4: projectile damage + difficulty tuning".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain what the projectile prefab was missing and why no message ever fired
  • Defend your choice of trigger versus solid, and say which callback name each one requires
  • Explain how a bullet reaches the player's health method, and why the null guard matters
  • Explain which sign of the number hurts, why it is that sign in your own method, and what the other sign would do
  • Name the four difficulty knobs, where each one lives, and your value for each
  • Say how many turrets the scene shipped with, and how many you added
  • Break this feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this feature came from, and where you would reread it
  • Run a silent playtest and make one evidence-based change
  • Commit and push
